_meta.what: What riders call each direction of travel on each troncal corridor.
_meta.why: A compass bearing cannot name a direction in Bogotá. The street grid is not square to true north, so a corridor keeps ONE name for its axis along its whole length even where the road bends: Calle 26 is oriente/occidente even where its bearing swings north, and the NQS stays norte/sur through the Soacha stretch that physically runs east-west. Deriving the name from the bearing produced 'nororiente' for the Caracas and disagreed with signage on eight of the twelve corridors.
_meta.source: Answered station-pair by station-pair by the maintainer, 2026-08-12, as the deciding authority. Each corridor was posed as a concrete trip ('Bus de Calle 76 - Heroes'), and the 24 answers cover all 1444 boardable services at the 140 troncal stations. Two were corrected on review because a corridor's two ends came back with names that were not opposites; the pair that flushed them out is recorded below.
_meta.how: `axisBearing` is the mean heading of the `positive` end. Project a leg's bearing onto that axis: travelling with it takes `positive`, against it takes `negative`. A leg that leaves the corridor entirely (perpendicular, e.g. the bus that turns off Carrera 7 onto Calle 26 at Museo Nacional) takes the perpendicular pair instead — see `labelFor` in services/station_plan.ts.

corrections.note: Caracas would have read occidente one way and sur the other. Re-posed as 'Bus de Calle 76 - Héroes'.

corrections.asked: Bus de Museo Nacional - Centro Memoria
corrections.note: The example was the wrong bus: that one turns west onto Calle 26, so occidente was right for it but not for the group. Re-posed as 'Bus de Museo Nacional - K7 CL40', which climbs Carrera 7.
